newsitem.title: USA: SEC sues California firm for municipal bond fraud.
newsitem.headline: SEC sues California firm for municipal bond fraud.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission Monday sued securities brokerage First California Capital Markets Group Inc., capping a three-year municipal bond probe that divided the public finance community.
The SEC said it sued First California and two of its executives for allegedly defrauding investors who bought $69 million worth of municipal bonds.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, alleged that First California principal H. Michael Richardson and former manager Derrick Dumont lied to investors and omitted important information from bond offering documents about the risks investors faced.
The six-count complaint asks the court to order the underwriting firm and its executives to return "all ill-gotten gains" plus interest and to pay civil penalties, the SEC said.
Through an attorney, First California denied any wrongdoing and vowed to fight the SEC's lawsuit.
"First California, Mike Richardson and Derrick Dumont deny unequivocally the claims and charges made by the SEC," said their attorney, Charles Klinedinst.

"It is ironic that after three years of investigation involving literally dozens of witnesses, the SEC's charges come down to five bond issues that are all currently paying," Klinedinst said. "They've got nothing."
For nearly three years, the SEC has been investigating First California bond deals in Nevada County and in the cities of Ione, Avenal and Wasco, all located in central California.

David Bayless, the SEC's district administrator in San Francisco, said the lawsuit should send a message to other bond professionals that the commission is committed to "cleaning up the municipal securities market."
"By bringing this action against an underwriter, I think the commission is sending this message loud and clear," Bayless said.

The First California case was one of the SEC's first municipal bond investigations to target local governments. It sparked a heated debate in the municipal finance community over who should be held responsible when bond deals go bad.
SEC critics argue that local government officials are not sophisticated bond professionals and should not be held liable for complex transactions they do not understand.
Others say local elected officials need to spend more time reviewing bond deals and should be held accountable along with the bond professionals they hired.
For their part, Nevada County, Ione, Avenal and Wasco officials have denied any wrongdoing, insisting they relied on municipal bond experts to prepare and sell the bonds.
Sources said, however, that the local governments which issued the bonds and other professionals remain under investigation.
